prompt.context: Satellite imagery is used for a wide range of applications such as border control and military purpose (Defense & Intelligence), agriculture and forest monitoring (Living Resources), support to Oil & Gas and Mining industries (Natural Resources), infrastructure monitoring and support to arctic maritime transportation (Industry), real-estate and insurance (Services), and support to Local & Regional Planners, emergency services, and environmental studies (Public Authorities). Imagery distributors are intermediaries reselling imagery from several satellite operators. A Canada-based reseller of satellite imagery wants to accelerate its growth. The client is already an established actor on the Canadian Market.
prompt.question: The client is considering building a new ground station to directly receive imagery from satellites instead of receiving it from satellite operators. The ground station would receive imagery from one satellite only. What should they think about?

clarifying_info.q: What are the benefits of a direct ground station connection to a satellite?
clarifying_info.a: The ground station direct connection would allow: (1) Tasking the satellite in a very short time frame (30 min vs 6 hours currently), and (2) Receiving imagery in a very short time frame (10 min vs 6 hours currently).

clarifying_info.q: What type of imagery does the satellite provide — Optical or Radar?
clarifying_info.a: The ground station could be connected to either a satellite providing Optical or Radar imagery. Optical satellites use only one resolution; the newest Radar satellites can adapt and provide every resolution (High, Medium, or Low).

clarifying_info.q: What share of the Defense & Intelligence demand can the client address?
clarifying_info.a: At least 99.5% of the Defense & Intelligence demand comes from non-Canadian D&I organizations; the client therefore cannot address this demand.

framework: Market size: Is the opportunity viable? Is the market growing?
Potential benefits of the ground station: faster turnaround time, potential cost savings, improved image quality
Breakeven analysis: upfront CAPEX + ongoing OPEX vs. incremental revenue from the ground station
Competition: how will competitors react? Do others have ground stations?
Capabilities: what skills/resources are needed to build and operate the station?
Current & future segment/market size and current market share/revenues
Value proposition: why is faster turnaround better and for which segments?
Future market share/revenues with the ground station
Supply: satellites currently in-orbit, satellite lifetime considerations
Fit in satellite operator supply chain (mutual benefit)

questions.prompt: Which imagery segment(s) should the client target with its ground station? (Use Exhibit 2)
questions.guidance: The candidate should immediately identify that HR Optical is the largest segment by far ($342M). They should then note that Defense & Intelligence (D&I) represents a huge share, especially of HR Optical, and proactively ask about the origin of D&I demand. Upon learning that 99.5%+ of D&I demand is non-Canadian and therefore inaccessible to the client, they should re-assess which segments are viable.

questions.prompt: Now excluding D&I demand, which segment(s) should the client target? (Use Exhibit 3)
questions.guidance: With D&I excluded: HR Optical drops to $68M and MR Optical is $82M — making MR Optical the largest addressable segment in 2016. A good candidate uses the growth rates to project 2023 sizes. HR Optical at +148% reaches ~$169M; MR Optical at +91% reaches ~$157M. So HR Optical will be slightly larger by 2023, but MR Optical will represent a larger cumulative market over the 7-year period (assuming constant year-on-year growth). Both HR Optical and MR Optical are strong candidates. Radar is a single cumulative segment and smaller. A top candidate will flag the cumulative market insight.

math.setup: Apply growth rates to 2016 base (D&I excluded) to estimate 2023 market size
steps: HR Optical slightly larger in 2023, but MR Optical larger every year 2016-2022, so cumulative MR Optical market 2016-2023 is larger
math.answer: Both HR Optical and MR Optical are primary targets. HR Optical leads by 2023; MR Optical leads on cumulative 7-year market size.

questions.prompt: What factors should the client consider when choosing where to locate the ground station? (Brainstorming — use Exhibits 4 and 5)
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 4 (footprint circle) to understand coverage radius and mentally overlay it on Exhibit 5 (locations map). Key dimensions: (1) Market served — what industries/verticals are within the footprint (forest, farmland, mines, oil & gas, arctic shipping lanes)? (2) Build & operating costs — permafrost, iced ground, snowstorms, and remote logistics increase construction and maintenance costs. (3) Connectivity — ability to transmit imagery from the ground station to clients or a hub; Optic Fiber access is critical. Urban/suburban locations (Vancouver, Winnipeg) have fiber; arctic/remote locations do not.

questions.prompt: Should the client make the investment in the ground station? Calculate profits with and without the ground station and the incremental value. (Use Exhibit 6)
questions.guidance: A strong candidate recognizes this is an incremental analysis: compare profits with vs. without the ground station over the investment horizon. Client operating costs remain at 80% of revenues throughout. Ground station costs (CAPEX and OPEX) are additive. Candidate should think about discount rate even if told to ignore it, and flag it as a risk. The answer: cumulative profit with GS ($66.8M) exceeds cumulative profit without GS ($57.6M), so the investment is worth making — incremental profit over 8 years = +$9.3M.

math.setup: Compare profits with ground station vs. status quo, 2016-2023. CAPEX: Civil work $480K + Land $50K = $530K (Year 1), Antenna $5M split equally Year 1 ($2.5M) and Year 2 ($2.5M) → Year 1 total CAPEX $3.0M, Year 2 CAPEX $2.5M. OPEX (from Year 3): License $1.5M + Operations & Maintenance $0.3M = $1.8M/year. Client operating costs = 80% of revenues with GS.
steps: Year 1 (2016): Revenue w/GS $28.1M, OPEX $22.4M (80%), CAPEX $3.0M → Profit $2.6M; Status quo profit $5.6M; Delta -$3.0M
Year 2 (2017): Revenue w/GS $30.0M, OPEX $24.0M, CAPEX $2.5M → Profit $3.5M; Status quo profit $6.0M; Delta -$2.5M
Year 3 (2018): Revenue w/GS $36.0M, OPEX $28.8M (80%) + $1.8M GS OPEX = $30.6M → Profit $5.4M; Status quo profit $6.4M; Delta -$1.0M
Year 4 (2019): Revenue w/GS $43.2M, OPEX $34.6M + $1.8M = $36.4M → Profit $6.8M; Status quo profit $6.9M; Delta $0.0M
Year 5 (2020): Revenue w/GS $51.9M, OPEX $41.5M + $1.8M = $43.3M → Profit $8.6M; Status quo profit $7.4M; Delta +$1.2M
Year 6 (2021): Revenue w/GS $62.2M, OPEX $49.8M + $1.8M = $51.6M → Profit $10.6M; Status quo profit $7.9M; Delta +$2.8M
Year 7 (2022): Revenue w/GS $74.7M, OPEX $59.8M + $1.8M = $61.6M → Profit $13.1M; Status quo profit $8.4M; Delta +$4.7M
Year 8 (2023): Revenue w/GS $89.6M, OPEX $71.7M + $1.8M = $73.5M → Profit $16.1M; Status quo profit $9.0M; Delta +$7.1M
Cumulative profit w/GS: $66.8M; Cumulative profit status quo: $57.6M; Net incremental gain: +$9.3M over 8 years
math.answer: Cumulative profits with ground station ($66.8M) exceed status quo profits ($57.6M) by $9.3M over 8 years. The investment is financially justified, but the client breaks even only by Year 4 (2019) and the discount rate would reduce the NPV.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the client consider when choosing where to locate the ground station? Consider both the business opportunity and operational factors across the four candidate locations.

categories.name: Market Served
ideas: Coverage footprint determines which industries/verticals are reachable (agriculture, mining, oil & gas, arctic shipping, urban real estate)
Locations closer to economic activity hubs serve more paying clients
Arctic location covers arctic maritime shipping lanes (Industry vertical)
Southern locations (Winnipeg, Vancouver) cover agriculture, Energy & Natural Resources, Services

categories.name: Build & Operating Costs
ideas: Permafrost and iced ground increase civil construction costs
Arctic/remote locations face higher logistics costs for materials and equipment
Snow storms and extreme weather raise ongoing maintenance costs
Urban and suburban locations have lower construction and maintenance costs
Remote locations may require on-site power generation

categories.name: Connectivity & Data Transmission
ideas: Optic Fiber access is essential to transmit imagery to clients quickly
Vancouver and Winnipeg have Optic Fiber; arctic/remote locations do not
Without fiber, a separate connectivity solution (satellite backhaul) would be needed, adding cost and latency
Fiber availability aligns with the fast-turnaround value proposition of the ground station

categories.name: Strategic / Competitive
ideas: Location affects which satellite passes overhead and how frequently
Proximity to existing client base reduces sales and logistics friction
Risk of building in a heavily regulated area (border, military zone)
Potential to integrate the station into the satellite operator's own ground station network

recommendation: The client should proceed with building the ground station: cumulative profits with the ground station ($66.8M) exceed the status quo ($57.6M) by $9.3M over 2016-2023, with breakeven reached by Year 4 (2019).
Target HR Optical and MR Optical segments (D&I excluded); MR Optical is larger in the near term and cumulatively, HR Optical becomes slightly larger by 2023.
Preferred location should balance low build/operating costs, Optic Fiber connectivity, and proximity to addressable market demand (Winnipeg or Vancouver most attractive).
risks: Supplier lock-in: the station connects to a single satellite, creating dependency on one operator; risk if the satellite reaches end-of-life or better imagery becomes available from another satellite.
Discount rate not applied: factoring in time value of money would reduce NPV and potentially change the decision.
The investment could strain relationships with other satellite operators who currently supply imagery to the client.
Licensing risks: contract terms must be solid; loss of license removes the revenue premium.
D&I demand is large but currently inaccessible; changes in legislation or policy could open this market.
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on the satellite operator and secure a solid, long-term licensing agreement before committing.
Model the NPV with an appropriate discount rate to stress-test the business case.
Explore whether the ground station could be integrated into the satellite operator's own network of ground stations (mutual benefit, potential cost share).
Investigate whether future legislation could open D&I demand to Canadian resellers.
Evaluate Winnipeg (suburban, Optic Fiber, Humid Continental) and Vancouver (urban, Optic Fiber) as preferred locations based on cost and connectivity analysis.
